claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Controllers/ProductsController.cs (tag stage-1 = commit 83c0004): inside `public async Task<ActionResult<List<ProductDto>>> List()` on `ProductsController(DonHangDbContext db)` — `var products = await db.Products.Select(p => new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd)).ToListAsync();`. The fragment quoted in section 4 is character-for-character the source's, and `p` is a `Product` row from `db.Products`.

git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs | cat -A — lines 1-13 are byte-identical to the lesson's block: namespace, both comment lines, then `public sealed record` ProductDto(int Id, string Name, int PriceVnd), OrderItemDto(int ProductId, int Quantity, int UnitPriceVnd), OrderDto(int Id, int CustomerId, string Status, DateTimeOffset PlacedAt, List<OrderItemDto> Items), CreateOrderItemRequest(...), CreateOrderRequest(List<CreateOrderItemRequest> Items). The file continues at line 15 with LoginRequest/LoginResponse, which the prose's "the first records in the file" now covers honestly.

git show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs — `public sealed class Product { public int Id { get; set; } public required string Name { get; set; } public int PriceVnd { get; set; } }`. Exactly three properties, the same three `ProductDto` lists, so section 2's "`Product` only has `Id`, `Name`, and `PriceVnd`" and section 5's "a coincidence of today's code" both hold.

Entities.cs @ stage-1: `public sealed class OrderItem` declares OrderId, ProductId, Quantity, UnitPriceVnd (all `{ get; set; }`). Dtos.cs: `OrderItemDto(int ProductId, int Quantity, int UnitPriceVnd)` — OrderId is the only dropped field. OrdersController.ToDto maps `i => new OrderItemDto(i.ProductId, i.Quantity, i.UnitPriceVnd)` and OrderItemDto occurs only nested inside OrderDto, which carries the order's own `Id` — so "a client reading an order already knows which order it asked for" is true of this code.

Entities.cs @ stage-1: `public sealed class Customer` has Id, `required string FullName`, `required string Email`, `required string City`, and `public string? PasswordHash { get; set; }` with the comment "Null until the customer sets a password; added by the AddPasswordHashToCustomers migration." The lesson's "alongside a customer's name and email" matches FullName/Email; City is also there, which "alongside" does not exclude.

configure-options.md, "Web defaults for JsonSerializerOptions": "PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase". customize-properties.md: "By default, property names and dictionary keys are unchanged in the JSON output, including case"; CamelCase = "First word starts with a lower case character. Successive words start with an uppercase character" (TempCelsius -> tempCelsius). ASP.NET Core formatting.md, on Mvc.JsonOptions: "configures PascalCase formatting instead of the default camelCase formatting". Both halves of the claim hold.

Settled two ways rather than through up.sh (it needs the Flutter SDK on the host). (1) The repo capture at this tag, outputs/stage-1/scripts/backend/auth-and-orders.txt, begins [{"id":1,"name":"Bàn phím cơ","priceVnd":1250000},... (2) I built and ran an ASP.NET Core 10 app (net10.0, SDK 10.0.300, AddControllers, no JSON options) returning Ok(new ProductDto(1, "Bàn phím cơ", 1250000)); the bytes were exactly {"id":1,"name":"Bàn phím cơ","priceVnd":1250000}, hexdump shows real UTF-8, no escapes. seed.sql has (1,Bàn phím cơ,1250000); Caddyfile proxies /api/v1/* to api:8080.

claim_verdicts.evidence: configure-options.md, "Web defaults for JsonSerializerOptions": "PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true". Confirmed by running: POSTing `{"Items":[{"ProductId":2,"Quantity":1,"UnitPriceVnd":450000}]}` to an ASP.NET Core 10 controller action taking `CreateOrderRequest` bound exactly as the camelCase body did (both echoed one item). Note the ledger entry has no sentence in the lesson behind it: the body only declines to cover the incoming direction, it never states that reading is case-insensitive.

issues.quote: would serialize that field too, unless every future change to `Customer` is checked against what every client already receives
issues.text: Unlisted claim, and the condition is false. Serializing `PasswordHash` does not depend on anyone checking anything: ASP.NET Core does not set DefaultIgnoreCondition, so `return Ok(customer)` writes "passwordHash":null for a customer with no password and the real hash for one with a password (I ran both against an ASP.NET Core 10 controller). As written, a junior can read it as "reviewing every change makes returning the entity safe" — the very misconception the bullet exists to kill, and the opposite of quiz q6's key, which says the field is serialized "null or not".
issues.fix: Replace the clause with the unconditional fact: "— returning `Customer` directly from any future endpoint would serialize that field too: it appears in the response as `passwordHash`, `null` or not." Then add a claim to .meta.json (kind behavior, version_key aspnetcore): "Returning the Customer entity from an endpoint serializes PasswordHash as a passwordHash field, including when it is null, because ASP.NET Core writes null properties by default."

issues.quote: deserialization turns it into a `CreateOrderRequest` before any of your code sees it
issues.text: Two unlisted points in one sentence. (1) "before any of your code sees it" is too strong for this repo: Program.cs runs app.UseMiddleware<ExceptionHandlingMiddleware>() and app.UseMiddleware<RequestLoggingMiddleware>() — code the same team wrote — before model binding reads the body. Summary line 3 already states it correctly ("before your endpoint code runs"), so the lesson disagrees with itself. (2) That POST /api/v1/orders binds its body to CreateOrderRequest is a repo fact no claim covers, though true: Create(CreateOrderRequest request).
issues.fix: Change to "...turns it into a `CreateOrderRequest` before your endpoint's code runs", matching summary line 3. Add a fact claim to .meta.json: "OrdersController.Create takes a CreateOrderRequest bound from the POST /api/v1/orders body", source DonHang.Api/Controllers/OrdersController.cs @ stage-1.

issues.quote: the default JSON options write every property name in camelCase for you
issues.text: Sections 3 and 4 both scope the rule to the outgoing direction ("written in camelCase for a response"); section 6's bullet and summary line 4 ("The default JSON options write each property name in camelCase") drop that scope. Unscoped, the sentence is not true of the pinned defaults in either neighbouring sense: System.Text.Json on its own leaves names unchanged ("By default, property names and dictionary keys are unchanged in the JSON output, including case"), and on the way in the same web defaults match case-insensitively rather than requiring camelCase.
issues.fix: Add the same two words used in sections 3 and 4 to both places: section 6 -> "the default JSON options write every property name in camelCase for a response"; summary line 4 -> "The default JSON options write each property name in camelCase for a response — `PriceVnd` becomes `priceVnd` — without being asked to."

issues.quote: A DTO is not the entity; something in the endpoint's own code has to build one from the other, field by field.
issues.text: "entity" is never defined. Core concepts says a DTO is kept separate from "whatever internal type the server uses", then section 4 switches to "the entity" and section 5 to "DonHang.Domain's entities" without saying the two words mean the same thing. I can guess it, but the lesson's whole point is DTO-versus-entity, so I am guessing at the main idea.
issues.fix: In the Core concepts DTO bullet, name it once: "...kept separate from the internal type (the entity) the server uses for the same thing."

issues.quote: **DTO** (data transfer object) — a plain type shaped for the wire, holding only the fields a client needs
issues.text: "shaped for the wire" / "on the wire" is jargon I have not met. It carries the definition of the one term this lesson teaches, and it is also in the title and in summary line 1, so I cannot skip it. The rest of the bullet ("only the fields a client needs") is what actually told me something.
issues.fix: In the DTO bullet, gloss it in place: "shaped for the wire — for the JSON that travels in a request or a response —".

issues.quote: Each `record` here is a type whose only job is to hold these named values — a shape, not behavior.
issues.text: The block declares `public sealed record ProductDto(int Id, string Name, int PriceVnd);` and the prose calls it "named values", but nothing says the names inside the parentheses ARE the type's properties. Everything after this depends on that: "one JSON field per property", "three fields, matching ProductDto's three properties", and quiz q3/q4. I had to assume it.
issues.fix: After "a shape, not behavior", add one sentence: "Each name in the parentheses is one property of that type — that is the list serialization walks."

issues.quote: it is what the serializer does to every property, every time, unless told otherwise.
issues.text: "unless told otherwise" opens a door and shuts it. I do not know whether telling it otherwise is something I will have to do, or how, and I spent time wondering whether I had missed it earlier in the lesson.
issues.fix: Replace "unless told otherwise" with "and nothing in this lesson changes it", so I know there is nothing missing.

issues.quote: Property names do not survive that trip unchanged going out.
issues.text: The camelCase rule is carefully limited to "going out", and the paragraph before it says a request body's JSON fills a `CreateOrderRequest`. So if I send a body myself, do I write `items` or `Items`? The text raises the question by saying "going out" and never answers it, and Try it only exercises a response.
issues.fix: Add one clause after "going out": say whether the same camelCase names are what an incoming body is expected to use, or say that incoming names are not covered here.

issues.quote: `ProductsController.List()`, from the last lesson, does exactly this: `new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd)`
issues.text: `ProductsController.List()` and the fragment `new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd)` are not in this lesson's code block, and `p` is never named. The following clause ("read off a `Product` row") lets me work out that `p` is the row, but only after a second read.
issues.fix: Change "one argument per property, read off a `Product` row" to "one argument per property, read off `p`, a `Product` row".

issues.quote: kept in one file separate from `DonHang.Domain`'s entities
issues.text: `DonHang.Api` and `DonHang.Domain` appear as the two places DTOs and entities live, but the text never says what they are — two projects, two folders, two namespaces? The separation is the point of the sentence, so I would like to know what is being separated.
issues.fix: Add three words at first use: "separate from `DonHang.Domain`, the project that holds the server's internal types".

issues.quote: ASP.NET Core's default JSON options write each property name in camelCase for a response
issues.text: "ASP.NET Core's default JSON options" — neither "ASP.NET Core" nor "JSON options" has been introduced to me. I can read it as "the framework decides this", but "options" sounds like a named thing I was supposed to have seen already.
issues.fix: Say it without the unintroduced noun: "by default, property names are written in camelCase for a response".

issues.quote: 1. With the lab running, run `curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/1`.
issues.text: "With the lab running" assumes a step nothing in this lesson or in what I was told before states. If I do not already know the command that starts it, step 1 fails with nothing to look at, and the concrete Expected result cannot help me.
issues.fix: Name the start command in step 1, or say "with the lab started as in the earlier lesson" so I know where to look.

issues.quote: A plain type shaped for the wire, holding only the fields a client needs
issues.text: The correct option is a word-for-word copy of the Core concepts bullet, so I can match it by sight without understanding anything. The other three do not even look like definitions of a type.
issues.fix: Reword option a so it is not verbatim, e.g. "A type written only to carry the fields a client needs, separate from the server's internal type".

issues.quote: False, because `Product` and `ProductDto` are stored in different files, and types in different files can never be merged.
issues.text: Two distractors defeat themselves with absolutes ("always redundant", "can never be merged") and the correct option is the longest and most careful one. I would pick it from shape alone, without having read the lesson.
issues.fix: Make option d plausible instead of absurd, e.g. "False, because `Product` is also used by code outside the API", so shape alone does not decide it.

issues.quote: `Get(int id)` reads one `Product` row from the database
issues.text: The step names `Get(int id)` and a database read, and the lesson shows neither — it names `ProductsController.List()`, and its diagram starts at `Product entity` with no database in it. I can still order the four, but I am ordering something I was never shown.
issues.fix: Reword the step to what the lesson shows: "The endpoint reads one `Product` row".

issues.quote: `201` belongs to a successful `POST` that creates something, from the REST-resources lesson
issues.text: The explanation for option d credits `201` to "the REST-resources lesson", which taught me resources and HTTP methods, not what `201` means; this lesson's Connections points forward to a later lesson for status codes. Being told I already learned something I did not makes me distrust my other answers. (The scenario's `return Ok(customer);` is also unexplained, though guessable.)
issues.fix: Drop "from the REST-resources lesson" from explanation d and say status codes are covered in a later lesson.
